title: Nandini, the sage's cow
hookLine: gods steal a sage's wondrous cow, and a curse that can't be unsaid is shaped instead: why Hindus honor the cow
carry: gau mata: the cow, honored as a giver
tomorrow: why has the great river stopped flowing?
last: MOKSHA: RELEASE FROM THE ROUND OF BIRTHS.

cards: His wife has just told Shantanu she is Ganga, and that his seven lost sons were the Vasus, gods under a curse. His promise is broken, and she's about to go.

So he asks the one thing he still can: what did the Vasus do, that they had to be born as men and die as babies? Ganga answers him before she leaves. Her answer starts on a mountainside, with a sage and his cow.

teach.b: The sage is Vasishtha. He keeps his hermitage on a mountain slope, and he owns a wondrous cow named Nandini, one of the wish-giving cows of Hindu story. One day the Vasus come wandering there with their wives.

One wife sees the cow and wants her, not for herself, but for a friend on earth, a princess, so her friend might stay young and free of illness. Her husband is a Vasu named Dyu. He knows whose cow this is.

teach.h: DYU TAKES HER TO PLEASE HIS WIFE.
teach.b: But to please his wife, with his brothers helping, he takes her.

Vasishtha comes back to an empty pasture, sees with a sage's inner sight what happened, and curses the Vasus: they will be born on earth as men. The Vasus beg him to take it back. He can't unsay the curse.
But he can shape what follows.
The seven who helped will be freed soon after they're born. Dyu, who took the cow, will live a long life on earth: virtuous and learned, devoted to his father, and with no children.
So the eighth son, the one Shantanu saved by speaking, is Dyu himself. Two teachings sit in this. The first is why the story turns on a cow.

teach.h: GAU MATA: THE COW, HONORED AS A GIVER.
teach.b: In Hindu tradition the cow is honored as a giver, gau mata, mother cow: like a mother, she feeds others and asks little. To rob a sage of his cow was a grave wrong, grave enough to bring gods down to earth.
The second is karma, measured to fit: the helpers are freed fast, and the one who took the cow carries the longest life.

how: Many Hindus honor the cow as gau mata, mother cow; some households and temples keep and care for cows, and on festivals such as Gopashtami cows are bathed, decorated and fed. Vasishtha's Nandini belongs to the wondrous cows of Hindu story, said to give what is wished for.

games.q: you're Vasishtha. the Vasus who stole your cow come begging you to lift your curse. what do you do?
o: let it stand, but shape what follows.
games.why: he can't unsay it, but he shapes it: seven freed soon after birth, and Dyu, who took the cow, to live a long, virtuous life with no children.

practice: Before your next meal or cup of tea, count the givers who brought it to you: the cow, if there's milk, the farmer, the hands that cooked or poured. Name each one silently, and say thank you once, out loud or under your breath.
Many Hindus pause to offer food before eating; this is a small way of noticing what was given.
